response.query: How to implement translation/back-translation, glossing conventions, and pilot screening to detect lexical or cultural bias in prompts and glosses?
response.answer: Translation/back-translation involves translating text forward and then back to check for bias; glossing conventions standardize morphological breakdowns; pilot screening detects lexical or cultural bias in translations.

results.title: Writing Exercise: Lexical translation
results.content: # Writing Exercise: Lexical translation. Take a poem in a foreign language that you can pronounce but not necessarily understand and translate it word for word with the help of a bilingual dictionary. Alternately, take a poem in your own language, translate it into another language, then translate it back. Enter text in the first field "Original text". Check "audo detect" or choose the original language and choose the language to translate to. Your translation will appear in the second field. Take the translation and put it in the "Original text" field and translate it into another language. Repeat this with a few languages. Finally, translate the text back into your language.

results.title: Cultural and Linguistic Bias of Neural Machine Translation Technology (Chapter 4) - Translation Technology in Accessible Health Communication
results.content: There are three sets of natural language features annotated on the original English and back-translation health materials: multiple semantic categories using the university of Lancaster Semantic Annotation System (USAS); word frequency bands (WFB); and lexical dispersion rates (LDR), with the last two based on the British National Corpus. In order to further improve the performance of the optimized classifier F75, we performed statistical analyses of the dispersion rate features and semantic features in the two sets of English mental health materials: labeled as 0, indicating no back-translation associated with statistically increased negative emotions, and labeled as 1, indicating back-translations with strong negative connotations in one or more of the three languages – Chinese, Hindi, and Spanish (Table 4.4). To review, then, we have succeeded in developing a high-performing relevance vector machine (RVM) classifier to predict the likelihood of a certain English health text being translated by Google as having statistically increased negative connotations when compared to the original English text. And as discussed, we have developed machine learning classifiers mitigate this undesirable effect by detecting English mental health information that might lead to biased translation in the three languages. By contrast, a low-sensitivity classifier is relatively unlikely to identify potentially problematic original English mental health information – that is, to screen out any materials that are not safe and suitable for neural machine translation. As for classifiers with high specificity, they are more suitable for identifying original English mental health texts which are suitable for neural machine translation, at least for the three languages we studied, Chinese, Hindi, and Spanish. Accordingly, we have developed Bayesian machine learning classifiers to assist with the probabilistic detection and prediction of socially biased neural machine translation outputs, using computational modeling and pairwise comparisons of original English and back-translations of neural machine translation outputs on anxiety disorders in Chinese, Hindi, and Spanish. These models provided informative probabilistic predictions of the likelihood that an English text on anxiety disorders would be translated by Google into one of the three languages with subtle but strong negative connotations – again, because neural machine translation favors natural language translations.

results.title: Glossing Conventions
results.content: # The Afranaph Project: Anaphora in the African Languages. **Afranaph Glossing Conventions – Revised September, 2016**. This is a list of the most commonly used glosses in the Afranaph database. Words are separated by spaces on original text, morpheme breakdown and gloss lines. A single morpheme in the morpheme breakdown is bounded on either side by an empty space (at the beginning or end of a word) or by a dash or dashes if it is word internal, and if an indivisible morpheme expresses a combination of glosses, then the glosses corresponding to the single morpheme are separated by a period, as in the example below. At various points we diverge from the Leipzig glosses either because they are not available for certain kinds of morphemes, they are not specific enough for certain kinds of distinctions, or they are not distinct enough to allow for optimal searches in the database. Searching for CAUS will find all three glosses, but the distinction between CAUS1 and CAUS2 is included because many Bantu languages have two affixes that have been characterized (by some) as causative, although their effects differ in interesting ways (and ways that interact with patterns of anaphora). 3 FUT: In languages that have temporally distinct future morphemes, FUT is distinguished as FUT1 (temporally closest to PRS), FUT2 (next temporally closest)…FUTn. Many Bantu languages have such systems. 5 PST: In languages that have temporally distinct past morphemes, PST is distinguished as PST1 (temporally closest to PRS), PST2 (next temporally closest)…PSTn. Many Bantu languages have such systems. 7 REFL: Many markers that are interpreted as reflexive are not glossed with REFL because we are particularly interested in the morphological and semantic properties of distinct forms of reflexive marking. We only use REFL when the morpheme in question is not a verb affix and has no other meaning in another use in the language, e.g., when a reflexive argument consists of a pronoun compounded with a root that means ‘body’, the gloss is PRN-BODY, or in some cases, the capitalized morphology of the root in the language (particularly when more than one root can for a reflexive argument).

results.title: Cross-Cultural Research and Back-Translation – The Sport Journal
results.content: The purpose of this paper is to provide researchers with an overview of issues regarding the cross-cultural study as well as the adapting or translating an instrument. Finally, item response theory (IRT) applied to a variety of translated tests offers the possibility for cross-cultural researchers to solve the problem of measurement inequivalence as well as to discover the cultural and/or lingual differences (Ellis, 1989). Sireci and Berberoglu (2000) attempted to evaluate translated-adapted items by means of bilingual respondents because there is no guarantee that the different language versions of instruments are equivalent (in their research, they utilized an English-Turkish version of a course evaluation form). Therefore, cross-cultural researchers should be cognizant of the numerous potential problems, such as construct, method, and item bias that could affect the results of studies. After identifying the possible bias, cross-cultural researchers should use appropriate statistical analysis techniques including confirmatory factor analysis and item response theory to examine, avoid, or eliminate the bias.

results.title: Leipzig glossing rules - Language Miscellany
results.content: The glossing conventions provide standard ways of abbreviating possible descriptions of a language’s morphological patterns, but do not help linguists decide between different descriptions. Hyphens separate segmentable morphemes, both in the example and in the gloss. If elements are morphologically bound but constitute distinct prosodic or phonological words, a single space may (optionally) be used together with the hyphen in the foreign language (but not in the gloss). When a single foreign-language element is glossed by more than one metalanguage element (words or abbreviations), the gloss separates these elements with periods (.). There are various reasons why one foreign-language element may correspond to more than one element in the gloss. | backslash \ | to separate the category label from the rest of the gloss if a grammatical property in the foreign-language is signalled by a morphophonological change (eg ablaut, mutation, tone alternationc) |. | square brackets [ ] | enclosing a gloss element with no corresponding overt element in the object language text.
